channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: Dropout from individual cognitive behavioral psychotherapy for schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined dropout rates from individual cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs) in randomized clinical trials (RCTs), addressing a key barrier to treatment effectiveness in outpatient settings.
FINDINGS: Across 13 RCTs (16 CBT arms, n=865), the pooled dropout rate was ~20% (one in five participants). Substantial heterogeneity was observed between arms. Exploratory meta-regression found no significant associations with sociodemographic, clinical, or treatment-related moderators due to limited power.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate in strength (systematic review of RCTs) but limited by heterogeneity and underpowered moderator analyses. The 20% dropout rate is clinically meaningful, but causal factors remain uncertain. The lack of significant moderators likely reflects insufficient data rather than true absence of effect.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should anticipate ~20% dropout in individual CBT for SSDs and monitor engagement closely. Current evidence does not support tailoring CBT based on the explored moderators. Further research is needed to identify predictors of dropout and strategies to reduce it.

item.title: Non-pharmacological interventions for perinatal parental depression and anxiety: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The review asks which non-pharmacological interventions delivered to both parents during the perinatal period are most effective for reducing depression and anxiety in either parent. It is a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of 36 RCTs (n = 15 477 parents).
FINDINGS: For depression, multicomponent interventions showed a standardised mean difference (SMD) of –0.34 (95% credible interval [CrI] –0.60 to –0.08) and psychosocial interventions –0.25 (95% CrI –0.43 to –0.07). For anxiety, multicomponent interventions had SMD –0.48 (95% CrI –0.66 to –0.29) and parent–child interaction interventions –0.19 (95% CrI –0.36 to –0.03). Evidence certainty was rated low to moderate.
INTERPRETATION: The networks were sparse, most comparisons were indirect, heterogeneity was substantial, and the overall certainty of evidence was low to moderate. Therefore, the ranking should be regarded as provisional. Larger, head-to-head RCTs are needed before firm recommendations can be made.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence tentatively favours multicomponent family-centred programmes for perinatal parental depression and anxiety, but the small effect sizes and low certainty mean routine practice should await more robust trials.

item.title: Effect of Digital Technology-Based Interventions on Core Symptoms and Cognitive Function in Children With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether digital technology-based interventions (computer-based training, serious video games, exergames, virtual reality) improve core ADHD symptoms and cognitive function in children, addressing uncertainty about their efficacy and generalisability.
FINDINGS: Thirty-seven RCTs (n≈3,000) were pooled. Digital interventions significantly reduced core symptoms (SMD −0.31, 95 % CI −0.48 to −0.14; P=.02) and improved cognition (SMD −0.33, 95 % CI −0.51 to −0.15; P=.04). Effects were strongest for serious video games on core symptoms and for computer-based training on cognition. Subgroup analyses suggested larger benefits in children <10 years and with ≤8 weeks of intervention.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate-sized but heterogeneous (I² ≈60–70 %). Risk of bias was generally low to moderate; publication bias could not be ruled out. Effect sizes are modest and likely below commonly accepted thresholds for clinically meaningful change in routine care. The findings are sensitive to intervention type, age, and duration, limiting generalisability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Digital interventions may offer small adjunctive benefits, particularly for younger children or short courses, but are not yet a replacement for established treatments. Clinicians should set realistic expectations and monitor outcomes individually.

item.title: PROMATER: protocol for a randomized controlled trial of a digital self-guided intervention to promote perinatal mental health and reduce self-criticism.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Perinatal mental health is a public health priority, with self-criticism as a transdiagnostic vulnerability and self-compassion a protective factor. This Brazilian RCT protocol (PROMATER) tests a 3-week digital self-guided intervention targeting these processes in 130 pregnant women (28–34 weeks gestation), using an active control to isolate specific effects.
FINDINGS: The trial randomizes participants 1:1 to PROMATER (6 modules on self-compassion/mindfulness) or an active control (same structure without transdiagnostic modules). Primary outcomes are the Compassionate Self-Responding (CSR) and Uncompassionate Self-Responding (USR) scores from the Self-Compassion Scale, assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and 3-month postpartum. Secondary outcomes include depression, anxiety, quality of life, social support, and mother-infant bonding. Analysis will use Linear Mixed Models (ITT principle).
INTERPRETATION: As a protocol, no results are available yet. The design is robust (randomization, blinding of participants/data analysts, active control, ITT analysis), but external validity hinges on recruitment feasibility and adherence in routine care. The incremental benefit of targeting self-criticism/self-compassion over psychoeducation alone remains unproven until outcomes are reported. If effective, the brief, scalable digital format could address access gaps in Brazil.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No clinical change yet—await trial outcomes. If positive, PROMATER could offer a low-cost, accessible adjunct to perinatal mental health care, but implementation would require integration into existing services and evaluation of real-world effectiveness.

item.title: Exploring the Neural Mechanisms of Acupuncture Stimulation in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Protocol for a Randomized, Sham-Controlled, Multimodal Neuroimaging Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a protocol for a randomized, sham-controlled neuroimaging trial (2×2 design) aiming to explore acute neural mechanisms of acupuncture in 70 participants (35 with ASD, 35 typically developing controls) using functional near-infrared spectroscopy and electroencephalography. The study addresses whether acupuncture modulates resting-state network metrics and frontal band power differently in ASD versus controls.
FINDINGS: The trial is ongoing; to date, 23 ASD and 21 controls have been enrolled. Primary outcomes will compare resting-state network metrics and relative band power in frontal areas by diagnosis and intervention (verum vs sham). Secondary outcomes will assess group × intervention interactions on these neural markers.
INTERPRETATION: This is a well-designed, sham-controlled protocol with clear stratification and multimodal neuroimaging, which strengthens internal validity. However, as a protocol paper, no results are available yet; thus, efficacy and effect sizes remain unknown. The small sample size and exploratory nature limit power to detect meaningful clinical effects. The study may clarify acute neural correlates of acupuncture but cannot yet inform clinical practice.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this study does not change clinical practice. It may lay groundwork for future trials but should not influence decisions about acupuncture use in ASD until efficacy and safety are demonstrated in adequately powered, peer-reviewed studies.

item.title: Multidimensional Evaluation of the Efficacy of a Comprehensive Ayurveda Approach as an Add-On to Conventional Therapy in Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder: Protocol for a Randomized, Open-Label, Parallel-Group, Active-Controlled Clinical Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a protocol for a randomized, open-label, parallel-group, active-controlled clinical trial (n≈80) in children aged 6–15 years with DSM-5–defined autism spectrum disorder (ASD) at a single Indian centre. It aims to test whether adding two Ayurvedic formulations (Saraswata Ghrita and Ayush Manas) to conventional therapy improves behavioural symptoms, cognition, adaptive functioning, parental quality of life, and exploratory inflammatory biomarkers over 6 months.
FINDINGS: The trial is ongoing; as of July 2026, 20 children had baseline data, 14 had completed 90-day follow-up, and 2 had finished the 6-month intervention. Planned analyses include repeated-measures ANOVA or Friedman tests with α=0.05. No efficacy results are yet available.
INTERPRETATION: Because this is a protocol with no published outcomes, readers should regard all conclusions as preliminary. The open-label design, single-centre recruitment, and lack of placebo control risk performance and detection bias. Biological endpoints are exploratory and not powered for definitive inference. Until peer-reviewed results appear, the clinical value of adjunctive Ayurveda in ASD remains unproven.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, there is no direct evidence to change practice; clinicians should continue to rely on established behavioural and developmental interventions while awaiting the trial’s outcome.

item.title: Subcutaneous Esketamine in Adolescents with Severe Depressive Episodes: A Five-Case Series.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This five-case observational series examined the feasibility, tolerability, and short-term symptom changes of adjunctive subcutaneous esketamine in adolescents (15–17 years) with severe depressive episodes and limited prior treatment response. The study aimed to describe acute tolerability and preliminary efficacy signals in a real-world specialized outpatient setting.
FINDINGS: All five patients completed the eight once-weekly sessions (0.5–1.0 mg/kg). MADRS trajectories were heterogeneous: one remission, three partial improvements, and one no sustained benefit. MADRS Item 10 (suicidal ideation) decreased in four patients, and MADRS Item 8 (anhedonia) decreased in four. Transient mild dissociative symptoms and blood pressure elevations occurred in one and some patients, respectively; no severe adverse events, hospitalizations, or suicide attempts were reported during the 8-week protocol.
INTERPRETATION: This uncontrolled case series suggests feasibility and short-term tolerability of subcutaneous esketamine in adolescents under close monitoring, but the uncontrolled design, small sample, and heterogeneous outcomes preclude causal inference. The observed reductions in suicidal ideation and anhedonia-related symptoms are preliminary and should be regarded as hypothesis-generating. Larger, controlled pediatric trials with standardized dosing, suicide-specific assessments, and longer follow-up are required to establish efficacy, safety, and durability of effect.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine use of subcutaneous esketamine in adolescents; it should remain investigational pending robust trials. Clinicians considering off-label use must weigh unproven benefits against uncertain long-term risks and ensure close monitoring for adverse effects.

item.title: Rethinking treatment motivation in addiction care: executive functions and personality over clinical severity- a cross-sectional study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study examined whether treatment motivation in individuals with alcohol or substance use disorders (n=190, inpatient at ADATC, April–August 2025) is better predicted by executive functions and personality traits than by clinical severity indicators.
FINDINGS: Addiction severity did not significantly predict treatment motivation (β not reported). Executive functions—especially goal-directedness—were the strongest predictors (β and effect size not provided). Personality traits showed that higher neuroticism and extraversion were associated with greater motivation, while higher psychoticism was linked to lower motivation (correlations not quantified).
INTERPRETATION: The study’s cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. The lack of effect sizes and confidence intervals limits assessment of clinical significance. Confounding by unmeasured variables (e.g., concurrent psychosocial interventions) is possible. The findings suggest cognitive and personality factors may shape motivation, but replication with longitudinal data and clearer quantification is needed before practice changes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify altering routine assessment or treatment based solely on these preliminary associations; further research is required to determine whether targeting executive functions or personality traits improves motivation and outcomes in addiction care.

item.title: Associations between month/season of birth and health outcomes: an umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This umbrella review synthesised systematic reviews and meta-analyses to assess whether month or season of birth is associated with long-term health outcomes, focusing on objectively measured conditions and grading the strength of evidence. It included 10 meta-analyses covering 614 pairwise associations across diverse health outcomes.
FINDINGS: Among 45 statistically significant associations, only one reached class II evidence: a modest increase in schizophrenia risk for January births (OR 1.05). Winter births were consistently linked to higher schizophrenia risk, while spring births showed associations with multiple sclerosis. Most other associations (autoimmune, oncological, perinatal) were graded as weak (class III–IV) due to small effect sizes or high heterogeneity.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is broad but largely weak; only schizophrenia shows a modest, relatively consistent signal. Methodological quality varied, and many associations reflect small effects with substantial heterogeneity or bias risk. The grading framework helps distinguish plausible signals from spurious findings, but causal inference remains uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not support using birth month/season to guide individual risk assessment or prevention strategies. Clinicians should remain aware that any observed associations are small and not clinically actionable at present.

item.title: A Primary Care E-Health Family Intervention for Risk Behaviors in Hispanic Youths: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description: IMPORTANCE: Culturally tailored, evidence-based family interventions that can be effectively delivered within pediatric primary care settings may provide a scalable approach for preventing risk behaviors among Hispanic adolescents. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether the online eHealth Familias Unidas Primary Care (eHealth FUPC) program reduced drug use and increased condom use in Hispanic youth and to examine family functioning as a mediator.

item.title: Paracetamol overdose: systematic review of case reports and national toxicological data (2018-2023).
item.description: OBJECTIVES: Paracetamol is widely used as an analgesic and antipyretic, but its accessibility also makes it a frequent drug in overdose cases. Increasing rates of intentional paracetamol poisoning, particularly among adolescents, raise public health concerns. This study aimed to examine recent patterns of paracetamol overdose and identify risk groups for intentional self-poisoning. METHODS: A systematic review of published case reports (2018-2023) describing paracetamol overdose was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library.

item.title: Advantage of cerebellar intermittent theta-burst stimulation in Alzheimer's disease (ACT-AD): study protocol for a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: The cerebellum plays a crucial role in cognitive processing and thus presents a promising therapeutic target for Alzheimer's disease (AD). This trial aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of long-term, neuronavigated cerebellar intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) in patients with AD. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: The ACT-AD trial is a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled study involving 100 participants with mild-to-moderate AD across 4 centers in China.

item.title: Predictors of improvement in personal recovery and activity engagement among mental health service users following a group-based sensory modulation intervention.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Mental health service users often have sensory processing difficulties affecting activity engagement and personal recovery. Since interventions targeting this area are scarce, a group-based sensory modulation intervention was developed. To determine in which settings and for whom this intervention has clinical value, this study aimed to investigate whether sociodemographic and clinical baseline characteristics were associated with improvement in personal recovery and activity engagement.

item.title: White matter signatures of addiction diverge across opioids, cannabis and nicotine and predict impulsive choice in cannabis dependence.
item.description: White matter (WM) microstructure is implicated in the neurobiology of substance use disorders (SUDs), yet direct comparisons across substance-dependence syndromes remain scarce. It is also unclear whether WM abnormalities relate to impulsive decision-making and substance use severity.

item.title: Mapping the psychosis spectrum - imaging neurosubtypes from multiscale functional network connectivity.
item.description: Psychosis exhibits marked neurobiological heterogeneity that is not adequately captured by symptom-based diagnoses. Although prior efforts have identified subgroups, it remains unclear how latent disease variability manifests within the brain's multiscale intrinsic functional organization and whether these patterns can be leveraged to systematically identify biologically driven subtypes of psychosis.

item.title: The genetic orchestra of autism and its intersections with epilepsy, intellectual disability, and ADHD.
item.description: Autism is a complex condition with marked phenotypic variability and a multifactorial etiology orchestrated by diverse genetic and environmental influences. In this review, we dissect what we refer to as autism's "genetic orchestra", spanning from the high-impact "soloists", de novo and ultra-rare variants with large effect sizes, to the "polyphonic background" of common variants which individually exert modest effects but collectively have significant impact.

item.title: Childhood Trauma, Recent Stressors, and Risk of Depression Relapse in Late-Life Depression.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Recent stressors have been linked to poor outcomes of late-life depression (LLD), including relapse. Emerging evidence has linked adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) to the occurrence of LLD. We sought to examine the relationships between recent exposure to stressful life events and ACEs with relapse following remission among older adult. METHODS: In this cohort study, depressed older adults (age ≥65) were provided standard antidepressant medications by a study psychiatrist.

item.title: Staged bilateral reverse sural artery flap reconstruction for severe frostbite of both feet in a patient with schizophrenia: A case report.
item.description: RATIONALE: Bilateral, weight-bearing heel defects after frostbite are difficult to reconstruct, and outcomes depend heavily on postoperative off-loading and patient cooperation. We report a limb-salvage strategy for severe bilateral foot frostbite that occurred during acute psychosis in a patient diagnosed with schizophrenia. PATIENT CONCERNS: A 25-year-old man developed acute psychotic symptoms and walked barefoot in subzero conditions for about 12 hours, resulting in deep frostbite of both heels and multiple toes.

item.title: Neuronal IL-18 Signaling in the Medial Habenula Contributes to Schizophrenia-Like Behavioral Deficits via ERK-Associated BDNF Suppression.
item.description: Current antipsychotics for schizophrenia (SCZ) are notably ineffective against the debilitating cognitive and negative symptoms, creating a major therapeutic gap. Neuroinflammation in the medial habenula (MHb) is implicated in SCZ; however, the underlying cell-type-specific mechanisms remain unknown. This study aimed to determine whether pathologically elevated neuronal interleukin-18 (IL-18) in the MHb contributes to schizophrenia-like behavioral abnormalities through ERK-associated downregulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF).

item.title: Regional and national burden of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in Asia, 1990-2023: a Global Burden of Disease Study 2023.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) represents a substantial lifelong economic and functional burden, yet comprehensive assessments of its burden in Asia have been limited. In this study, we quantified the burden of ADHD across Asia at both regional and national levels. METHODS: We estimated the burden of ADHD across 34 Asian countries from 1990 to 2023 using data from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023. ADHD was defined as the presence of six or more inattention or hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms lasting ≥ 6 months.

item.title: Bionic sleep therapy combined with multimodal management for chronic insomnia with alcohol withdrawal-related symptoms: A case report.
item.description: RATIONALE: Patients who use alcohol as a sleep aid may experience withdrawal-related insomnia and hyperarousal, which can reinforce continued drinking. Bionic sleep therapy (BST) is an exploratory intervention using intravenous anesthetic and sedative agents under close monitoring to induce a brief, controllable, sleep-like state. It may provide short-term support for sleep initiation during early alcohol withdrawal.

item.title: A composite measure of healthy lifestyle and the association with suicidal behaviors in Chinese young people aged 10-24 years: Results from a school-based survey in Zhejiang Province.
item.description: OBJECTIVES: Smoking, alcohol drinking, dietary habits, physical activity, screen time, and sleep duration have been examined separately in relation to suicidality. Based on these behaviors, this study aimed to develop a composite measure of a healthy lifestyle, and to explore its associations with suicidal behaviors among Chinese young people aged 10-24 years. METHODS: Data were obtained from 2022 Zhejiang Youth Risk Behavior Survey, in which 27,059 students aged 10-24 years completed an anonymous questionnaire designed to assess the health behaviors.

item.title: Suicidal Behaviour and Non-Suicidal Self-Injury in Adolescents With Childhood Sexual Abuse: Associated Clinical Factors and Psychological Correlates.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Childhood sexual abuse is a major developmental trauma associated with elevated risk for non-suicidal self-injury and suicidal behaviour in adolescence. Yet, it remains unclear whether abused adolescents show distinct motivational profiles for self-injury and how depression and emotion dysregulation jointly relate to suicide risk.

item.title: Implementing a Telehealth Perinatal Depression Prevention Program: Perspectives of Rural and Urban Clinical Staff.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Nurses are key stakeholders in telehealth intervention implementation. Nurses are also instrumental in the management of perinatal depression, a common complication during pregnancy and postpartum. Telehealth interventions are a promising approach to addressing perinatal depression; however, its successful integration into routine maternal care remains challenging, particularly across diverse clinical settings.

item.title: Determinants of Psychological Readiness to Return to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Psychological and physical factors influence recovery after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction (ACLR). However, the relative contributions of psychological, subjective, and objective recovery measures to psychological readiness for return to sport remain unclear. OBJECTIVE: To identify psychological, subjective, and objective recovery factors associated with psychological readiness to return to sport approximately 6 months after ACLR. DESIGN: Cross-sectional study. SETTING: University laboratory.

item.title: Association between viewing more media war content and higher intention to use cannabis in adolescents: the indirect effect of post-traumatic stress.
item.description: BACKGROUND: The ongoing Israeli-Palestinian conflicts increased the risk of multifront war, especially with bordering countries like Lebanon. In addition, with the increased use of media, graphic war content is easily transmitted to adolescents without regulation. This has significantly impacted their lives, mentally and physically, leading to the search for coping mechanisms like cannabis use. However, the exact link between war media exposure and cannabis use intention is still uncertain.

item.title: HPSC-derived mesenchymal stromal cells ameliorate murine autistic-like phenotypes through activating oxytocinergic neurons.
item.description: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heritable neurodevelopmental disorder marked by social deficits, repetitive behaviors, and psychiatric comorbidities. Despite its rising global prevalence, effective treatments remain elusive. Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) offer therapeutic promise for ASD, although their mechanisms are unclear. Here, we show that induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived MSCs alleviate anxiety, grooming, and social impairments in Shank3B knockout mice, a monogenic ASD model.

item.title: Gray matter subtyping with SuStaIn reveals neuroanatomical patterns in autism spectrum disorder.
item.description: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heterogeneous, and structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies have reported both increased and decreased gray matter volume relative to typically developing controls. This variability may obscure distinct neuroanatomical patterns in conventional group-level analyses. It therefore motivates subtyping approaches that can characterize neuroanatomical heterogeneity beyond conventional group-level analyses.

item.title: Links of fitbit-derived sleep architecture and fragmentation with ADHD symptoms and externalizing behaviors in adolescents.
item.description: Sleep disturbances are linked to adolescent externalizing behaviors and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms. However, few studies have examined associations between objectively measured sleep architecture and these behavioral outcomes. This study investigated whether specific sleep stages and fragmentation are associated with externalizing behaviors and ADHD symptoms in a large U.S. population-based cohort.

item.title: Examining the association between autistic traits and psychopathology in the general population: are there sex differences?
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Autistic traits (ATs) are linked to increased vulnerability to psychopathology. While sex differences are studied in clinical autism, little is known about these associations in the general population. This study examines sex-specific associations between ATs and psychopathology in a community sample of adolescents and young adults. METHODS: Data from 788 participants (475 females), aged 15-35 years (mean = 17.48 ± 3.60) in the TwinssCan cohort were used.

item.title: Parental Mealtime Practices in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Comparative Study.
item.description: ImportanceFeeding difficulties are highly prevalent among children diagnosed with autism and can significantly affect family well-being.

item.title: Prevalence of adult attention-deficit/ hyperactivity disorder symptoms among university students and their relation to sleeping duration, time management skills, and academic performance.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental condition that often persists from childhood into adulthood and is characterized by symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. In university students, these symptoms may negatively affect time management and academic performance. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of adult ADHD symptoms among university students at Jazan University, Saudi Arabia, and to examine their associations with time management skills and academic performance.

item.title: Functional Listening Difficulties in Children With ADHD: Associations With Language Abilities.
item.description: OBJECTIVE: Listening difficulties are commonly reported in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and are often interpreted as manifestations of inattention. However, it remains unclear whether functional listening difficulties are related to broader language abilities or whether they differ across ADHD subtypes. The present study examined the association between functional listening difficulties and language abilities in children with ADHD and explored whether these relationships vary between predominantly inattentive and combined subtypes.

item.title: Digital Media, Genetics, and Risk for ADHD Symptoms in Children: A Longitudinal Study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Children spend significant amount of time using digital media (DM), and longer exposure may increase attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-related symptoms, although findings are mixed. We investigated longitudinal association between different types of DM use and ADHD-related symptoms in school-aged children, accounting for genetic predisposition and socioeconomic status. METHODS: This study included children from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development Study, followed annually for four years.

item.title: Recent and Cumulative Cannabis Use and Sleep in Middle-Aged Adults.
item.description: IMPORTANCE: Cannabis is widely used and often promoted as a sleep aid, but evidence of its long-term implications for sleep is limited. OBJECTIVE: To examine the associations of cumulative cannabis exposure from young adulthood to middle age and recent cannabis use with objective and subjective sleep outcomes in middle age.

item.title: Suicide-Related Responses From AI Chatbots Through Application Programming Interfaces and Consumer-Facing Apps: Observational Cross-Sectional Comparative Study.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) chatbots are frequently used for mental health-related questions, including suicide-related queries. User interfaces (UIs) may include additional safety controls not present in direct application programming interface (API) access (eg, moderation rules that flag or block harmful content, crisis refusal templates, or system-level instructions).

item.title: SOGC Clinical Practice Guideline No. 471: Alcohol and Pregnancy.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a national clinical practice guideline (GRADE method) from the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SOGC) updating standards for screening, brief intervention, and referral for alcohol use in pregnant women and women of childbearing age. It synthesises evidence from 2018–2026 across Medline, EMBASE and CENTRAL to inform obstetric and primary care providers.
FINDINGS: The guideline recommends universal screening for alcohol use with validated tools (e.g., AUDIT-C) and brief interventions for all pregnant women and women planning pregnancy. It advises expedited referral pathways to alcohol cessation services and prioritised access to specialist support. Evidence quality was graded using GRADE, with most recommendations rated as moderate to low certainty due to heterogeneity in study designs and populations.
INTERPRETATION: As a guideline, internal validity is high in terms of methodological rigour (GRADE framework, systematic search), but external validity depends on local healthcare system capacity for referral and follow-up. The strength of recommendations is tempered by the low-to-moderate quality of underlying evidence, particularly for pharmacological interventions during pregnancy. The document does not quantify effect sizes or absolute risk reductions, so clinical significance remains inferred rather than empirically demonstrated.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should adopt routine screening and brief interventions for alcohol use in pregnancy and preconception care, ensuring clear referral pathways to addiction services. The lack of robust effect estimates means centres should monitor local outcomes when implementing these recommendations.

item.title: The effects of virtual reality interventions on outcomes related to well-being among autistic children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The clinical question is whether virtual reality (VR) interventions improve subjective well-being (SWB) or psychological well-being (PWB) in autistic children, using randomized controlled trials (RCTs) synthesized in a systematic review and meta-analysis.
FINDINGS: VR showed a positive but nonsignificant effect on SWB-related outcomes (g = 0.37, 95% CI [-0.03, 0.78], p = 0.07), while a statistically significant positive effect was found for PWB-related outcomes (g = 0.45, 95% CI [0.27, 0.63], p < 0.05). The meta-analysis included 10 RCTs, with 70% raising some risk-of-bias concerns and only eight effect sizes contributing to the PWB estimate.
INTERPRETATION: Confidence in the PWB result is limited by risk-of-bias concerns, small numbers of contributing studies, and heterogeneity in interventions and outcomes. The SWB finding is not statistically significant, so no firm conclusions can be drawn. Larger, well-controlled RCTs with standardized outcome measures are needed before VR can be recommended for routine use.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence suggests potential benefit of VR for psychological well-being in autistic children within research settings, but not yet for routine clinical practice; clinicians should await more robust trials before adopting VR for well-being outcomes.

item.title: Skin and Brain in Bipolar Disorder: A Review of Dermatologic-Psychotropic Drug Interactions.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines bidirectional dermatologic–psychotropic drug interactions in patients with bipolar disorder, focusing on how systemic dermatologic medications may destabilise mood and how mood stabilisers/antipsychotics may provoke clinically important cutaneous adverse reactions. It synthesises case reports, observational studies and pharmacovigilance data indexed to June 2026, but no randomised trials were identified.
FINDINGS: Dermatologic agents such as isotretinoin, systemic corticosteroids and methotrexate have been linked to mood destabilisation in susceptible individuals. Conversely, lithium and lamotrigine carry dermatologic risks including acneiform or psoriasiform eruptions, hidradenitis suppurativa and severe cutaneous adverse reactions. No quantitative effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is entirely observational and heterogeneous (case reports, series, pharmacovigilance), so causality cannot be established and effect sizes remain unknown. Strengths include broad coverage of drug pairs and explicit acknowledgment of gaps. Limitations include lack of controlled data, potential publication bias and unclear generalisability beyond bipolar populations. Clinically meaningful magnitudes of risk cannot be quantified from this review.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Until better evidence emerges, clinicians should screen for prior psychiatric episodes and cutaneous drug reactions, counsel patients about possible bidirectional risks, and monitor closely when initiating or escalating high-risk therapies; shared decision-making across specialties is advised.

item.title: Prevalence of mental health outcomes among trans and gender diverse adults: a global systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This global systematic review and meta-analysis synthesised 207 studies (n=134 071) to estimate current/lifetime prevalence of depression, anxiety, PTSD, suicidality and non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) among trans and gender-diverse adults, addressing gaps in prior reviews that often focused on youth or selected samples.
FINDINGS: Pooled prevalence estimates were 40.1 % (95 % CI 35.6–44.8) for depression, 29.8 % (20.3–40.2) for anxiety and 23.6 % (14.9–33.5) for PTSD. Past-12-month rates were 43.1 % (38.9–47.3) for suicidal ideation, 9.3 % (7.7–11.0) for suicide attempts and 26.1 % (20.4–32.2) for NSSI. Non-binary participants appeared to have higher rates, and estimates varied by assessment method, recruitment setting and region.
INTERPRETATION: The large, global dataset strengthens confidence in the elevated mental health burden among trans adults, though heterogeneity in assessment tools and recruitment settings limits precision. The absence of general-population comparators in most studies precludes direct risk ratio estimation; nonetheless, the absolute prevalences are markedly higher than general-population benchmarks. Funding sources were not reported, and selection bias cannot be ruled out in clinic-based samples.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support the need for accessible, gender-affirming mental health services and routine screening for depression, suicidality and NSSI in trans adults, with particular attention to non-binary individuals and regional disparities.

item.title: Revisiting the link between childhood adversity and stress-sensitive brain regions in psychosis and bipolar disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis investigated whether childhood adversity (CA) is associated with gray matter volume (GMV) reductions in stress-sensitive brain regions (hippocampus, amygdala, prefrontal cortex) in individuals with psychotic disorder (PD) or bipolar disorder (BD). The study synthesized findings from structural brain imaging studies to clarify inconsistent prior results.
FINDINGS: The review included 29 studies (n=3056; mean age 36.6±16.1; 47% female) of fair methodological quality with high heterogeneity. Most studies reported negative associations between CA and GMV, particularly in prefrontal regions. However, meta-analyses of 5 studies found no significant association between CA and hippocampal volume (p≥0.66), and 4 studies showed no association with amygdala volume (p≥0.87). Findings for the hippocampus and amygdala were largely null or inconsistent.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests that CA is not consistently linked to hippocampal or amygdala volume reductions in PD/BD, despite many individual studies reporting negative associations. The stronger and more consistent pattern emerged in prefrontal regions, though high heterogeneity and fair study quality limit firm conclusions. The meta-analytic results are robust for the hippocampus and amygdala (no effect detected), but cortical findings remain preliminary and warrant cautious interpretation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support a consistent neuroanatomical signature of CA in limbic structures among PD/BD patients. Clinicians should not assume hippocampal or amygdala atrophy is a direct consequence of CA in these populations. Further high-quality, longitudinal research is needed before considering structural brain changes as biomarkers of adversity in psychiatric care.

item.title: Estimating the Economic Value of Supported Online Parent-Led Cognitive Behavioral Therapy to Prevent Child Anxiety Problems: Economic Evaluation of the MYCATS Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study assessed the cost-effectiveness of a parent-led online supported cognitive behavioural therapy (OSI+TS) versus usual school practice (USP) for preventing anxiety in 4–7-year-olds identified by universal screening, using data from the MYCATS cluster RCT (n=865) with a 12-month follow-up.
FINDINGS: Children in the OSI+TS arm gained 0.021 (95 % CI 0.010–0.033) and 0.043 (95 % CI 0.021–0.064) QALYs under UK adult and Australia adolescent tariffs, respectively, at an extra cost of £244.16. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios were £11 462 and £5 701 per QALY, with 88.2 % and 99.3 % probability of being cost-effective at the £20 000 threshold.
INTERPRETATION: The cluster-randomised design and prespecified economic analysis plan strengthen internal validity, and ICERs fall well below NICE thresholds. However, the absolute QALY gains are small and the perspective is limited to NHS/PSS costs; societal spill-over and long-term outcomes remain unexamined. The short 12-month horizon and reliance on tariff-based QALYs also limit interpretability for routine child psychiatry.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: OSI+TS appears economically attractive within current thresholds, but clinicians should note the modest health gains and the lack of evidence beyond one year; implementation should be monitored for real-world uptake and sustained benefit.

item.title: Initiation of aripiprazole once-monthly using a two-injection start in adult patients diagnosed with schizophrenia: real-world views and experiences of Italian healthcare professionals.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This pan-European, non-interventional, cross-sectional online survey assessed Italian healthcare professionals' (HCPs) views and experiences regarding the two-injection start (TIS) initiation of aripiprazole once-monthly 400 mg (AOM 400) in adult patients with schizophrenia, a method designed to simplify treatment initiation without prolonged oral supplementation.
FINDINGS: Responses from 108 Italian HCPs (47.2% of participants) showed that poor treatment adherence (81.5%), patient preference (50.0%), and disease relapse (42.6%) were common reasons for using AOM 400-TIS. Barriers included patient reluctance to receive two injections (36.1%), concerns about tolerability (24.1%), and safety concerns (23.1%). Most HCPs reported satisfactory patient outcomes (85.2%), ease of administration (82.4%), and a safety/tolerability profile similar to the traditional one-injection start (69.4%).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides descriptive insights into HCP perspectives but lacks comparative data or patient outcomes, limiting causal inferences. Selection bias may exist due to voluntary participation, and the cross-sectional design precludes assessment of long-term effects. While HCPs generally viewed AOM 400-TIS favorably, the absence of objective clinical metrics or patient-reported outcomes weakens the evidence. Further research is needed to validate these perceptions with clinical efficacy and safety data.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence suggests AOM 400-TIS is perceived as practical and well-tolerated by Italian HCPs, particularly for patients with adherence issues, but definitive clinical benefits remain unproven. Clinicians should consider patient preferences and tolerability concerns when choosing initiation methods, while awaiting more robust data.

item.title: Applying a Behavioral Fit Analysis with Sexual Minority Youth at Risk for Suicide.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review and conceptual paper addresses the elevated suicide risk among sexual minority (SM) youth (ages 15–24) and proposes a behavioral fit analysis framework to integrate minority stress and social drivers of health into suicide risk assessment and treatment planning. It synthesizes literature on minority stress and existing assessment tools, illustrating application via a fictional case example.
FINDINGS: The paper summarizes evidence that SM youth face disproportionate suicide risk due to minority stress and discrimination. It introduces a behavioral fit analysis to tailor evidence-based suicide interventions by incorporating social determinants linked to SM identity. A fictional case demonstrates how this framework guides individualized treatment planning.
INTERPRETATION: This is a narrative review with illustrative case material, not empirical research. It offers a conceptual model rather than quantitative outcomes, so no effect sizes, p-values, or confidence intervals are reported. The strength lies in highlighting the relevance of social drivers of health in suicide prevention for SM youth, but the lack of empirical validation and reliance on a single fictional example limit internal validity and generalizability. External validity is uncertain as the framework has not been tested in real-world clinical settings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The proposed behavioral fit analysis may help clinicians consider minority stress and social context when assessing and treating suicidal SM youth, but it should be viewed as a preliminary framework. Clinicians should await empirical evaluation before adopting it as standard practice.

item.title: Development and preliminary evaluation of a group adaptation of the Unified Protocol for Transdiagnostic Treatment of Emotional Disorders in adolescents (UP-A) in a Spanish public mental health center.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study adapted the Unified Protocol for Transdiagnostic Treatment of Emotional Disorders in Adolescents (UP-A) into a group format and evaluated its feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary effectiveness in a Spanish public outpatient mental health setting. This open-label, single-arm pilot study included 31 adolescents (mean age 14.03; 87.1% female).
FINDINGS: 80.65% of participants completed the 16-session group intervention. High satisfaction and therapeutic alliance were reported by adolescents and parents. Significant improvements were observed in adolescent-reported emotional symptoms (effect size not reported) and emotion regulation strategies, alongside parent-reported reductions in depressive symptoms. Clinician ratings showed reduced diagnostic severity and improved functioning.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary due to the single-arm design, lack of a control group, small sample size, and retrospective trial registration, which raises concerns about selection bias and confounding. While the high completion rate and positive outcomes suggest feasibility and acceptability, the absence of randomization and blinding limits internal validity. The lack of effect sizes and confidence intervals precludes assessment of clinical significance. Further randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm efficacy.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The results suggest potential for group-based UP-A in public mental health settings, but current evidence is insufficient to recommend routine adoption. Clinicians should await confirmatory trials before considering this approach over established treatments.

item.title: The utility of animal models in hiPSC-based studies of autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a common and heritable neurodevelopmental condition. This systematic review (PRISMA-guided) examined how often animal models or animal-derived cells are still used alongside human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) research in ASD, questioning whether such animal use is necessary.
FINDINGS: Out of 207 hiPSC-based ASD studies (2009–2024), 79 (38.16%) also involved animals or animal-derived cells. Nearly half used animal models to study ASD neurobiology, while others employed animals for unrelated purposes (e.g., teratoma assays to confirm pluripotency or extracting primary astrocytes for co-culture, which may introduce confounding variables).
INTERPRETATION: The review suggests that animal use in hiPSC-based ASD research is frequent and sometimes unnecessary, potentially undermining the ethical and translational rationale for reducing animal experiments. However, the study does not assess the scientific contribution of animal components or whether their exclusion would compromise study validity. The review is limited by its descriptive nature and lack of critical appraisal of individual study designs or outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For clinicians, this review highlights a gap between the ethical goal of reducing animal use in ASD research and current practices. It does not directly inform patient care but underscores the need for clearer justification when animals are included in hiPSC-based studies.

item.title: Working with goals in youth mental health and substance use service: A review of current practice guidelines and recommendations.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines practice guidelines and recommendations for working with goals in youth mental health and substance use services (ages 10–25), focusing on therapeutic relationships, shared decision-making, and equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI). It synthesizes academic and clinical guidebooks published between 2003 and 2023 to assess how current practices embed EDI and cultural safety.
FINDINGS: The review identified 53 publications and distilled four themes: (1) semi-structured goal-setting with routine outcome monitoring; (2) youth- and family-centered engagement strategies; (3) conceptual integration of goals within therapy; and (4) a growing but still limited emphasis on EDI and cultural safety. No quantitative outcomes or effect sizes were reported.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this study provides a qualitative synthesis rather than empirical evidence. Strengths include broad coverage of guidelines and explicit attention to equity, but limitations include lack of systematic quality assessment, absence of quantitative data, and potential selection bias in included sources. The clinical recommendations remain conceptual, with uncertain generalizability and no direct evidence of improved outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: While the review supports adopting collaborative, youth-informed goal-setting practices, it does not provide measurable benefits or validated frameworks. Clinicians may consider integrating routine outcome monitoring and EDI principles, but should await empirical validation of these approaches before expecting measurable improvements in youth mental health outcomes.

item.title: Abnormalities of intrinsic brain activity in late-life depression: a meta-analysis of resting-state functional imaging studies.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined resting-state functional neuroimaging studies to identify consistent abnormalities in intrinsic brain activity in late-life depression (LLD) compared with healthy controls (HC). The clinical question was whether reproducible neural signatures exist that could clarify neuropathology and potentially aid diagnosis or treatment development.
FINDINGS: Thirteen studies (476 LLD patients vs 394 HC) were meta-analysed using anisotropic effect-size seed-based d mapping. Higher activity in LLD was found in the left fusiform gyrus (FG), right parahippocampal gyrus (PHG) and right middle frontal gyrus (MFG), while lower activity was observed in the left supplementary motor area (SMA), left superior frontal gyrus (SFG) and left postcentral gyrus (PoCG). Subgroup analyses by functional index and statistical correction showed largely consistent patterns, with additional involvement of the left superior occipital gyrus (SOG) in corrected analyses.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate in size but methodologically heterogeneous (varied imaging indices, correction methods, and small samples). The use of anisotropic effect-size seed-based d mapping improves robustness, yet the findings remain correlational and cannot establish causality. The reported regions are plausible but effect sizes are not quantified numerically in the abstract, limiting assessment of clinical significance. External validity is uncertain because included studies may overrepresent specific LLD subgroups and settings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest potential neural correlates of LLD that could inform future diagnostic or therapeutic targeting, but they do not yet support changes in routine clinical practice. Clinicians should await larger, longitudinal studies with harmonised imaging protocols before considering any neuroimaging-based interventions.

item.title: Neural mechanisms of guided internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy for children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a protocol for a prospective multimodal MRI study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study aims to investigate the neural mechanisms of guided internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy (ICBT) in children with ADHD using multimodal MRI, addressing a gap in understanding how ICBT affects brain structure and function. It is a protocol for a prospective study embedded within an ongoing randomized, sham-controlled ICBT trial, involving approximately 60 children with ADHD and typically developing (TD) controls for baseline comparisons.
FINDINGS: The study will compare pre- and post-intervention MRI scans (structural, resting-state functional, and diffusion tensor imaging) in children with ADHD randomized to ICBT or sham control. Baseline MRI data from TD children will serve as a reference. Analyses will focus on intervention-related neural changes and associations between baseline MRI markers and clinical treatment response.
INTERPRETATION: As a protocol, this study has not yet produced results, so no findings or effect sizes are available. The design is strong in its randomized, sham-controlled framework and multimodal MRI approach, which could provide valuable mechanistic insights. However, external validity will depend on the representativeness of the sample and the clinical setting. The study’s novelty lies in exploring neural predictors of treatment response, but results are pending.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This research could eventually identify neural biomarkers predicting ICBT response in children with ADHD, potentially personalizing treatment. However, until results are published, no clinical changes should be made based on this protocol alone.

item.title: Aortitis with eosinophilia as a rare complication of clozapine treatment ‒ a case of a patient with paranoid schizophrenia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a single case report describing a 54-year-old woman with treatment-resistant paranoid schizophrenia who developed aortitis with eosinophilia as a rare adverse effect of clozapine therapy. The report highlights an atypical and previously undocumented complication of clozapine.
FINDINGS: The patient developed inflammatory changes in the aorta (aortitis) accompanied by eosinophilia while on clozapine. Symptoms resolved after discontinuation of the medication. No quantitative data (e.g., laboratory values, imaging metrics, or follow-up duration) are provided in the abstract.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is extremely limited (a single case report) and lacks generalizability. There are no comparative data, effect sizes, or statistical analyses. The causal relationship between clozapine and aortitis is plausible but unproven in this context. The report serves primarily to raise awareness of a potential rare adverse effect rather than to establish causality or guide treatment decisions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This case suggests that clinicians should consider clozapine-induced aortitis in patients on clozapine who present with eosinophilia and unexplained vascular symptoms. However, given the rarity and lack of prior reports, routine screening for aortitis in asymptomatic patients on clozapine is not justified based on this evidence alone. Further investigation is needed before any practice change.
